extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidelines for evaluating and composing poetry focused on diction, metre, choice of subject (rustic life), and the representativeness of characters—largely a response to Wordsworth's preface and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the great masters
rubrics_metrics.description: The works of those who have stood the test of ages have a claim to that respect and veneration to which no modern can pretend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those great masters who have travelled the same road with success are the most likely to conduct others; longevity and stability of a work evince it is not suspended on the slender thread of fashion and caprice but bound to the human heart by sympathetic admiration. Use classic exemplars as reliable models for poetic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical sweep and stanzaic harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine interwoven harmony of the stanza ... forms a whole to the ear as truly as the more formal Spenserian stanza, but has a soft, flowing movement remarkably well fitted for the expression of thoughtful tenderness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metre and stanza for 'musical sweep' and harmony; long varied stanzas can still form an aural whole if they possess a soft flowing movement suited to sentiment. Example praise: Mr. Wordsworth's later poetry and certain unpublished lines exhibit such interwoven harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unmusical novelty in metre
rubrics_metrics.description: It is just enough to invent new metres, but come new metres which the world has lately been presented with will never live; they are as unmusical and not so spirited as a Chickasaw war-song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty of metre alone is not a virtue; metre must be musical and spirited. Be skeptical of new metres that lack natural musicality—such experiments often fail to endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry essentially ideal and generic
rubrics_metrics.description: I adopt with full faith the principle of Aristotle, that poetry is essentially ideal, that it avoids and excludes all accident; that its apparent individualities of rank, character, or occupation must be representative of a class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should embody generic, representative attributes (the common attributes of a class), not merely idiosyncratic features of a single gifted individual. The poet's aim is to show what may possibly happen (general things), not only particular historical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of rustic subject-matter is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet informs that he had generally chosen low and rustic life; but a low and rustic life is not necessarily a source of the essential passions of the heart for all persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'low and rustic life' as subject-matter is justifiable only for certain classes of poem and certain persons: it is applicable only where pre-existing education or sensibility allows nature's incidents to act as a stimulant. Do not assume rustic life is universally the best soil for passion or poetic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness vs apparent naturalness (imitation vs mere copy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure derived from rustic representation may be traced to three causes: (1) the naturalness of the things represented, (2) the apparent naturalness of the representation as raised by an imperceptible infusion of the author's own knowledge and talent, (3) the reader's feeling of superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective poetic imitation combines genuine naturalness of subject with the author's shaping infusion—so the work is imitation rather than bare copy. Beware pure mimicry lacking the poet's shaping intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and universal logic in poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A rustic's language, purified from all provincialism and grossness, and so far re-constructed as to be made consistent with the rules of grammar — which are in essence no other than the laws of universal logic — will not differ from the language of any other man of common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction should observe grammatical principles as expressions of universal logic to convey connections and general laws, not merely to list isolated facts. Polishing dialectal speech into grammatical, logical form often makes it intelligible and universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at general things (probability) not mere particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the poet is not to relate what has actually happened, but what may possibly happen, either with probability or from necessity. Poetry speaks more of general things, and history of particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poems by their success in capturing general, probable human truths and representative behaviors rather than by precise factual accuracy or individual biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character plausibility and representative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters of the vicar and the shepherd mariner ... have all the verisimilitude and representative quality that the purposes of poetry can require. They are persons of a known and abiding class, and their manners and sentiments the natural product of circumstances common to the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and portray characters whose manners, sentiments, and language plausibly follow from the circumstances of their class; where necessary, ensure that traits attributed to 'rustic' characters are explicable by education, local influences, or temperament, not merely asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for rustic inspiration (education/sensibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the human soul to prosper in rustic life a certain vantage-ground is prerequisite. Education, or original sensibility, or both, must pre-exist, if the changes, forms, and incidents of nature are to prove a sufficient stimulant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing rustic minds as refined or poetically responsive, provide (implicitly or explicitly) plausible grounds—education, religious reading (Bible, liturgy), or native sensibility—that explain their elevated perceptions; otherwise the depiction risks implausibility or moral hardening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual framing for persona-based lyrics
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'The Thorn' the poet acknowledges the necessity of an introductory poem, in which he should have portrayed the character of the person from whom the words of the poem are supposed to proceed: a superstitious man moderately imaginative, of slow faculties and deep feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a lyric or dramatic lyric uses a persona, provide framing or introduction that makes the speaker's character clear; otherwise lines meant to be characteristic of that persona may be misread or produce unintended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unmediated imitation of dullness or garrulity in lyric
rubrics_metrics.description: In a lyric poem ... it is not possible to imitate truly a dull and garrulous discourser, without repeating the effects of dulness and garrulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not slavishly reproduce the awkward, dull, or garrulous traits of a speaker in lyric form without counterbalancing or distancing them—better to let much proceed from the poet's imagination so the poem retains universal delight rather than mere mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-balance to prevent unintended burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: The idiocy of the boy is so evenly balanced by the folly of the mother, as to present to the general reader rather a laughable burlesque ... than an analytic display of maternal affection in its ordinary workings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting infirmity or folly alongside tenderness, ensure tonal balance so the reader perceives the intended pathos rather than a burlesque; provide descriptive cues or countervailing passages (e.g., beauty, sober lines) to steer interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer parts proceeding from the poet's imagination for universal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts — which might as well or still better have proceeded from the poet's own imagination, and have been spoken in his own character, are those which have given, and which will continue to give, universal delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositions or passages that arise from the poet's shaping imagination (rather than forced persona imitation) are likelier to produce universal emotional effect; prioritize imaginative construction to achieve wider resonance.
